title: Guided Project: Build a Small Office Network in Cisco Packet Tracer
subtitle: Build, address and secure a small office network in Packet Tracer: a router that hands out addresses by DHCP, a managed switch, PCs, and SSH-only management.
outcomes: Plan the addressing for a small office network, keeping fixed addresses out of the DHCP range
Configure a Cisco router as the office's default gateway and DHCP server
Secure a router and a switch with hostnames, hashed passwords, a warning banner and SSH-only remote access
Verify the network with ping, ipconfig and show commands
prerequisites: Basic networking ideas: IP addresses, subnet masks and default gateways. No Cisco experience is needed. You need Cisco Packet Tracer (free with a Cisco Networking Academy account).
description: In this guided project you'll build a small office's network from scratch in Cisco Packet Tracer, the way a network technician would set one up for real. Three short lessons cover the plan, how DHCP hands out addresses, and what a router or switch needs before it can be managed safely over SSH. Then, in one hands-on lab, you'll cable a router, a switch, PCs and a printer, make the router the office's default gateway and DHCP server, give the switch a management address, and lock both devices down with an enable secret, a console password, a warning banner and SSH-only remote access. You'll prove every part works with ping, ipconfig and show commands, and your instructor reviews your results.

modules.title: Build the office network
modules.summary: Plan the network, learn what DHCP and SSH need, then build the whole office network in Packet Tracer and prove that it works and is locked down.

lessons.title: Plan the office network
objectives: Describe the office's topology and what each device does
Plan the office's addresses: the gateway, the fixed addresses and a DHCP range
key_points: The office network has a 2911 router as its default gateway (and, later, its link to the internet), a 2960 switch that connects everything, a printer and the staff PCs, all on one LAN.
One subnet, 192.168.10.0/24, gives 254 usable addresses: plenty for a small office, with room to grow.

Devices that others need to find at a fixed address get static addresses at the low end: the router 192.168.10.1, the switch's management address 192.168.10.2 and the printer 192.168.10.5. Addresses .1 to .10 are kept out of DHCP for them.
PCs and laptops get their settings from DHCP: an address from 192.168.10.11 upwards, the mask 255.255.255.0, the default gateway 192.168.10.1 and a DNS server.
Write the plan down before building: a table of devices, ports, addresses and how each gets its address prevents mistakes and documents the network for whoever looks after it next.

walkthrough.title: Lay out and cable the office

steps.do: In a new Packet Tracer file, add a 2911 router, a 2960 switch, three PCs and a printer (End Devices > Printer).

Rename the devices R1, S1, PC1, PC2, PC3 and Printer: click a device's name label in the workspace and type, or use Config > Display Name. This changes only the label; the router's and switch's own hostnames are set in IOS later.
With Copper Straight-Through cables, connect R1's G0/0 to S1's G0/1, PC1, PC2 and PC3 to S1's Fa0/1, Fa0/2 and Fa0/3, and the printer to Fa0/10.
Wait for the switch ports' lights to turn green.
steps.see: The router's link stays red: its interface is shut down until you configure it.

steps.do: Add a note with your address plan, using the Place Note tool in the toolbar, so the plan travels with the file.
Save the file as small-office.pkt.

lessons.title: DHCP and the default gateway
objectives: Explain how a PC gets its settings from DHCP
Configure a Cisco router as a DHCP server and check its leases
key_points: DHCP hands out addresses in four messages, DORA: the client broadcasts a Discover, a server answers with an Offer, the client broadcasts a Request for it, and the server confirms with an Acknowledgement. DHCP runs over UDP, on port 67 at the server and 68 at the client.
A lease gives the client an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers and a length of time; the client renews it before it runs out.

On a Cisco router, ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.10 keeps addresses out of the pool, and ip dhcp pool OFFICE, with network, default-router and dns-server lines, sets what to hand out.
show ip dhcp binding lists the leases the router has given, with each client's IP address and hardware (MAC) address; show ip dhcp pool shows how much of the pool is in use.

A PC that gets no answer from DHCP gives itself a 169.254.x.x link-local address, and Packet Tracer's IP Configuration window says that DHCP failed: check the cable, the router's interface and the pool.
The default gateway handed out must be the router's address on the same LAN; without it, PCs can reach each other but nothing beyond the office.

walkthrough.title: Turn the router into a DHCP server

steps.do: Open R1's CLI and type no at the initial configuration dialog. Name the router and give G0/0 the gateway address.
steps.code:
enable
configure terminal
hostname R1
interface g0/0
ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
no shutdown
exit

steps.do: Keep the fixed addresses out of DHCP.
steps.code: ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.10

steps.do: Create the pool. 8.8.8.8 is a public DNS resolver: nothing answers there inside Packet Tracer, but the PCs receive the setting.
steps.code:
ip dhcp pool OFFICE
network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0
default-router 192.168.10.1
dns-server 8.8.8.8
end

steps.do: On PC1, open Desktop > IP Configuration and choose DHCP.
steps.see: DHCP request successful., with IPv4 Address 192.168.10.11, Subnet Mask 255.255.255.0, Default Gateway 192.168.10.1 and DNS Server 8.8.8.8.

steps.do: See the lease on R1.
steps.code: show ip dhcp binding
steps.see: 192.168.10.11 with PC1's hardware address and the type Automatic.

steps.do: Check from PC1's Command Prompt.
steps.code:
ipconfig
ping 192.168.10.1
steps.see: The address and gateway from DHCP, and replies from R1 with TTL=255.

lessons.title: Secure the devices: passwords and SSH
objectives: Protect a router or switch with an enable secret, a console password, a banner and local user accounts
Configure SSH and turn off Telnet for remote management
key_points: enable secret sets the password for privileged EXEC mode and stores it as a hash; the older enable password stores it as plain text, so use enable secret.
The console port (line console 0) needs a password and login, so that someone with a console cable can't walk straight in; exec-timeout logs out sessions left idle.
service password-encryption hides plain-text passwords in the configuration with a weak, reversible scheme (type 7): it stops someone reading them over your shoulder, but isn't real protection.

Telnet sends everything, passwords included, as plain text, while SSH encrypts the session. SSH on IOS needs a hostname, a domain name (ip domain-name), RSA keys (crypto key generate rsa, at least 768 bits for SSH version 2, and larger is better) and a local user (username admin secret ...).
On the vty lines that carry remote sessions, transport input ssh allows SSH only and login local checks the local user accounts; ip ssh version 2 turns off the older SSH version 1.
banner motd shows a warning to everyone who connects, and copy running-config startup-config saves all of this so it survives a restart.

walkthrough.title: Harden R1 and allow SSH only

steps.do: Set the enable secret, hide the plain-text passwords and add a warning banner.
steps.code:
configure terminal
enable secret OfficeEnable26
service password-encryption
banner motd #Authorised access only.#

steps.do: Protect the console.
steps.code:
line console 0
password OfficeConsole26
login
exec-timeout 5 0
exit

steps.do: Give the router a domain name and a local user, and generate RSA keys.
steps.code:
ip domain-name office.test
username admin secret OfficeAdmin26
crypto key generate rsa
steps.see: The name for the keys will be: R1.office.test, then How many bits in the modulus [512]:. Type 2048 and press Enter, and the keys are generated.

steps.do: Use SSH version 2 only, and lock the remote-access lines to SSH with local accounts.
steps.code:
ip ssh version 2
line vty 0 4
transport input ssh
login local
exec-timeout 5 0
end

steps.do: Check SSH.
steps.code: show ip ssh

steps.do: From PC1's Command Prompt, connect over SSH as admin.
steps.code: ssh -l admin 192.168.10.1
steps.see: A Password: prompt (nothing shows as you type OfficeAdmin26), then the R1> prompt. Type exit to leave.

steps.do: Save, then read what's stored.
steps.code:
copy running-config startup-config
show running-config
steps.see: enable secret 5 followed by a hash, password 7 followed by scrambled text under line con 0, username admin secret 5, and transport input ssh under line vty 0 4.

lab.title: Build, address and secure the office network
lab.goal: Build the whole office network from the plan: a router that is the gateway and DHCP server, a managed switch, PCs that get their addresses automatically, a printer with a fixed address, and both network devices hardened and reachable only over SSH.
setup: Your small-office.pkt from the first lesson, or a new file
The starter file office-plan.txt: the address plan, cabling and the lab's example passwords

steps.do: Open small-office.pkt, or build the topology from office-plan.txt: R1 (2911) G0/0 to S1 (2960) G0/1, PC1 to PC3 on S1 Fa0/1 to Fa0/3 and the printer on Fa0/10, all with Copper Straight-Through cables.
On R1, set the hostname, address G0/0 and turn it on.
steps.code:
enable
configure terminal
hostname R1
interface g0/0
description Office LAN
ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
no shutdown
exit

steps.do: On R1, keep .1 to .10 out of DHCP and create the OFFICE pool.
steps.code:
ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.10
ip dhcp pool OFFICE
network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0
default-router 192.168.10.1
dns-server 8.8.8.8
exit

steps.do: Set PC1, PC2 and PC3 to DHCP in Desktop > IP Configuration, one after another.
steps.see: DHCP request successful. on each, with addresses 192.168.10.11, .12 and .13 in the order they asked.

steps.do: Give the printer its fixed address in its Config tab: gateway 192.168.10.1 under Settings, and under FastEthernet0, Static, 192.168.10.5 with mask 255.255.255.0.
On S1, set the hostname and a management address with a default gateway.
steps.code:
enable
configure terminal
hostname S1
interface vlan 1
ip address 192.168.10.2 255.255.255.0
no shutdown
exit
ip default-gateway 192.168.10.1

steps.do: Harden R1: enable secret, password encryption, banner and console.
steps.code:
enable secret OfficeEnable26
service password-encryption
banner motd #Authorised access only.#
line console 0
password OfficeConsole26
login
exec-timeout 5 0
exit

steps.do: Set up SSH on R1. At How many bits in the modulus, type 2048.
steps.code:
ip domain-name office.test
username admin secret OfficeAdmin26
crypto key generate rsa
ip ssh version 2
line vty 0 4
transport input ssh
login local
exec-timeout 5 0
end

steps.do: Harden S1 the same way, from its own configuration mode. A 2960 has 16 vty lines, so use line vty 0 15.
steps.code:
enable secret OfficeEnable26
service password-encryption
banner motd #Authorised access only.#
line console 0
password OfficeConsole26
login
exit
ip domain-name office.test
username admin secret OfficeAdmin26
crypto key generate rsa
ip ssh version 2
line vty 0 15
transport input ssh
login local
exit

steps.do: On S1, label the used ports and shut down the unused ones.
steps.code:
interface range fa0/1 - 3
description Staff PCs
interface fa0/10
description Printer
interface g0/1
description Uplink to R1
interface range fa0/4 - 9
shutdown
interface range fa0/11 - 24
shutdown
interface g0/2
shutdown
end

steps.do: Save both configurations.
steps.code: copy running-config startup-config

steps.do: From PC1, check its settings and reach every device: ping R1, S1, the printer and PC2 (at the address ipconfig shows on PC2).
From PC1, connect to R1 and then S1 over SSH, run show ip interface brief on each, and exit.
steps.code:
ssh -l admin 192.168.10.1
ssh -l admin 192.168.10.2

steps.do: From PC1, try Telnet to R1.
steps.see: The connection is refused or closed: R1 accepts only SSH.

steps.do: On R1, collect the evidence.
steps.code:
show ip dhcp binding
show ip interface brief
show ip ssh
show running-config

steps.do: On S1, collect the evidence.
steps.code:
show ip interface brief
show running-config

checks.text: All three PCs got addresses by DHCP from the pool.
The fixed addresses are kept out of the pool, and the printer answers at its fixed address.
PC1 reaches the router and the switch.
R1's G0/0 and S1's Vlan1 are up with the planned addresses.
Passwords are hashed or encrypted, and a warning banner is set.
SSH version 2 is enabled, and the vty lines accept only SSH with local accounts.
PC1 can manage R1 over SSH.
S1's unused ports are shut down.

lab.submit: Paste, in order: PC1's ipconfig and pings; the SSH sessions from PC1 to R1 and S1; the Telnet attempt; R1's show ip dhcp binding, show ip interface brief, show ip ssh and show running-config; and S1's show ip interface brief and show running-config.

files.content:
Small office network: address plan (192.168.10.0/24)

Device    Port              Address           Mask            How it gets it
R1        G0/0              192.168.10.1      255.255.255.0   static (the office's default gateway)
S1        Vlan1             192.168.10.2      255.255.255.0   static (switch management)
Printer   FastEthernet0     192.168.10.5      255.255.255.0   static, gateway 192.168.10.1
PC1-PC3   FastEthernet0     from .11 upwards  255.255.255.0   DHCP from R1

Kept out of DHCP: 192.168.10.1 to 192.168.10.10 (for devices with fixed addresses)
DHCP pool OFFICE: network 192.168.10.0/24, default router 192.168.10.1, DNS server 8.8.8.8

Cabling (Copper Straight-Through)
R1 G0/0  - S1 G0/1
PC1      - S1 Fa0/1
PC2      - S1 Fa0/2
PC3      - S1 Fa0/3
Printer  - S1 Fa0/10

Names and accounts (example passwords for the lab only: choose your own on real equipment)
Hostnames: R1 and S1        Domain name: office.test
enable secret: OfficeEnable26    console password: OfficeConsole26
Local user for SSH: admin, secret OfficeAdmin26

hints: If a PC says DHCP failed, check that R1's G0/0 is up (show ip interface brief) and that the pool's network line is 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0.
SSH needs all four pieces: a hostname other than the default, ip domain-name, RSA keys and a local username. show ip ssh says SSH is disabled until they're all in place.
If SSH asks for a password and then refuses it, check the username's spelling and that the vty lines say login local, not just login.
Locked out of a device's remote access? The CLI tab in Packet Tracer is the console, so the console password still lets you in.
